title: Train in Simulation, Deploy on a Real Robot: Microduck with Isaac Lab 3.0
gist: NVIDIA tutorial for training an open-source Microduck biped (Pollen Robotics and Hugging Face) to walk in Isaac Lab 3.0 with Newton, then exporting the policy to ONNX and deploying it on the real robot or Microduck Arena. Sim-to-real transfer rests on actuator modelling (BAM, backlash) and domain randomization, with training reaching up to 1.25M steps per second on 16 GPUs.

insights.claim: Microduck is a newly released affordable open-source bipedal robot from Pollen Robotics and Hugging Face, and its walking policy can be trained in NVIDIA Isaac Lab with Newton, exported as ONNX and deployed on the real robot.
insights.speaker: Oluwaseun Doherty
insights.so_what: Shows NVIDIA's simulation stack being pulled into the open-source Hugging Face robotics ecosystem, widening the Isaac Lab developer funnel.
insights.quote: Microduck is a newly released affordable open-source bipedal robot by Pollen Robotics and Hugging Face.

insights.claim: A walking policy trained in simulation must cope with the friction, delays and mechanical play of real robot servos, which is the core sim-to-real gap the tutorial targets.
insights.speaker: Oluwaseun Doherty
insights.so_what: Actuator realism, not just physics fidelity, determines whether simulated training transfers to hardware.
insights.quote: A walking policy trained in simulation must also handle the friction, delays, and mechanical play of real robot servos..

insights.claim: The Microduck pipeline runs from install, to training, to evaluation in a Newton visualizer, to ONNX export, to copying the file to the robot and loading it, with a path to share the policy on the Hugging Face Hub or enter Microduck Arena.
insights.speaker: Oluwaseun Doherty
insights.so_what: A reproducible end-to-end recipe lowers the barrier for hobbyist and academic robot-learning adoption.

insights.claim: Isaac Lab trains Microduck by running simulated environments in parallel on the GPU, and the tutorial's launch command uses 4096 environments with the RSL-RL library on the rough-terrain task.
insights.speaker: Oluwaseun Doherty
insights.so_what: GPU-parallel simulation is the compute-hungry step that drives NVIDIA GPU demand in robot learning.
insights.quote: Isaac Lab accelerates Microduck locomotion training by running simulated environments in parallel on the GPU.

insights.claim: Distributed Isaac Lab training on 16 GPUs can reach up to 1.25M steps per second with rough terrain and backlash enabled, speeding training and increasing robustness.
insights.speaker: Oluwaseun Doherty
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete throughput benchmark for multi-GPU robot-learning workloads.
insights.quote: we can reach up to 1.25M steps per seconds with rough terrain and backlash enabled

insights.claim: The tutorial deploys the policy trained on rough terrain, while the flat-terrain task is offered as an alternative, and the rough variant adds stairs, slopes and uneven ground.
insights.speaker: Oluwaseun Doherty
insights.so_what: Training on harder terrain is the chosen route to robustness on hardware.
insights.quote: We used the rough terrain for deployment

insights.claim: The Microduck policy takes 61 observation values and outputs 14 joint positions, and observation order, normalization and action scaling must stay identical between training, export and deployment.
insights.speaker: Oluwaseun Doherty
insights.so_what: Interface mismatches are a common silent failure in sim-to-real deployment.
insights.quote: The policy takes 61 observation values and outputs 14 joint-positions.

insights.claim: The tutorial uses Newton with the MJWarp solver and Newton-based Better Actuator Models (BAM) to model servo response, plus a backlash preset that converts position targets into realistic servo torques via firmware controller, motor electrical limits, friction and delay.
insights.speaker: Oluwaseun Doherty
insights.so_what: Actuator-level modelling is the differentiator being pushed to make simulation trustworthy for cheap servo hardware.

insights.claim: Domain randomization on each Microduck covers mass and centre of mass, ground friction, joint inertia, encoder offsets, battery voltage and sag, and command latency, along with terrain variation and pushes.
insights.speaker: Oluwaseun Doherty
insights.so_what: Lists the specific parameters that make a low-cost robot policy transferable.
insights.quote: we randomize the mass/centre of mass, ground friction, joint inertia, encoder offsets, battery voltage/sag and command latency

insights.claim: Backlash, the mechanical play in a gearbox when a joint changes direction, is randomized independently per joint to represent uneven wear, exposing the policy to differences it will meet on the real robot.
insights.speaker: Oluwaseun Doherty
insights.so_what: Per-joint randomization of wear addresses a real hardware failure mode that uniform noise would miss.
insights.quote: Backlash is the mechanical play in a gearbox

insights.claim: Isaac Lab's RSL-RL playback automatically exports both TorchScript (policy.pt) and ONNX (policy.onnx), and Microduck's onboard runtime loads only the ONNX file.
insights.speaker: Oluwaseun Doherty
insights.so_what: ONNX is the portable handoff format between NVIDIA training and edge robot runtimes.
insights.quote: Microduck’s onboard runtime loads ONNX policies.
insights.locator: 4. Evaluate the Microduck walking policy and export it to ONNX

insights.claim: Microduck Arena, a Hugging Face Space, accepts policies with 61 observation values, 14 action values and a maximum size of 64 MiB, and ranks them on shared challenges with a leaderboard.
insights.speaker: Oluwaseun Doherty
insights.so_what: Leaderboards create a community benchmark and engagement loop around a shared robot platform.
insights.quote: Arena accepts models with 61 observation values, 14 action values, and a maximum size of 64 MiB.

insights.claim: Deployment copies policy.onnx to the robot with scp and loads it with the robotctl tool while the robot is supported on a stand, with a command to reset to the default walking policy if needed.
insights.speaker: Oluwaseun Doherty
insights.so_what: A simple, safe rollback path is what makes open-source hardware deployment practical.
insights.quote: Support the robot on its stand, then load the walking policy.

insights.claim: The deployed policy shows robustness to falls: the real Microduck recovers its footing and resumes walking after being knocked over.
insights.speaker: Oluwaseun Doherty
insights.so_what: Fall recovery on real hardware is evidence that the sim-to-real recipe works.
insights.quote: Microduck recovers its footing and resumes walking after being knocked over.

insights.claim: NVIDIA positions Isaac Lab 3.0 as unlocking GPU-parallel robot learning across locomotion, dexterous manipulation and vision-based tasks, with extensible environments and configurable physics and rendering backends.
insights.speaker: Oluwaseun Doherty
insights.so_what: NVIDIA is framing Isaac Lab as the general platform for physical AI training, expanding demand beyond a single robot.
insights.quote: Isaac Lab 3.0 unlocks GPU-parallel robot learning across locomotion, dexterous manipulation, and vision-based tasks

insights.claim: Suggested next steps include a curriculum that increases terrain difficulty, head-camera depth perception tasks, Kuka-Allegro dexterous lift and reorient tasks, and custom environments using SimReady assets from SimReady Central Library.
insights.speaker: Oluwaseun Doherty
insights.so_what: Shows the adjacent workloads (perception, manipulation, assets) NVIDIA wants developers to grow into.
